title: Verbal complements
subtitle: -ing forms, infinitives, preparatory it and the subjunctive

blocks.intro: Verbs followed by an -ing form include:

blocks.text: Many verbs are followed by a preposition + **-ing** form.
blocks.note: Darren insisted **on going** to the party. · I'm looking forward **to meeting** your brother.

items: The verbs **feel, hear, see, notice, overhear** and **watch** can also be followed by an object + the bare infinitive (without **to**).
**I saw Martha cross** the road. (= I saw all of it.) · **I saw Martha crossing** the road. (= I saw part of it.)
When the verb and the gerund refer to different subjects, we can use an object pronoun or a possessive pronoun to make it clear.
**Do you mind me/my going** out with your sister?

blocks.text: They **caught him taking** money from the till.
**Can you afford to buy** that car?

blocks.intro: Verbs followed by a full infinitive include:

blocks.text: My sister **advised me to tell** Jim the truth.

blocks.intro: Verbs followed by object + full infinitive include:

blocks.text: The teacher **let the class leave** early.

blocks.intro: Verbs followed by object + bare infinitive include:

blocks.text: In passive forms, **make** is followed by the full infinitive.
blocks.note: I **was made to apologise** to my sister. · Mum **made me apologise** to my sister.

items: The verbs **dare** and **need** can be used as modals, in which case they are followed by the bare infinitive.
**I don't dare tell** Simone what happened. · **You needn't invite** Ralph if you'd rather not.

theory.title: Infinitive or -ing with little or no change in meaning

blocks.intro: These verbs can take an infinitive or an -ing form with little or no change in meaning:

theory.title: Infinitive or -ing with a change in meaning

rows.use: consider / imagine + infinitive · believe; think something is/was
rows.example: I've always **considered him to be** a friend.

rows.use: consider / imagine + -ing · think about
rows.example: We're **considering getting** engaged.

rows.use: forget + infinitive · not do something you were planning to do
rows.example: I **forgot to ask** Brian about the wedding.

rows.use: forget + -ing · not be able to remember a past event
rows.example: I'll never **forget asking** Helen to marry me.

rows.use: go on + infinitive · stop one action or subject of discussion and start another
rows.example: We chatted about the football for a while and then he **went on to tell** me about his divorce.

rows.use: go on + -ing · continue
rows.example: How can you **go on living** with Michael?

rows.use: like + infinitive · be in the habit of doing; think it right to do
rows.example: I **like to eat** with my family once a week.

rows.use: like + -ing · enjoy
rows.example: I **don't like being spoken to** in such a rude manner.

rows.use: mean + infinitive · intend
rows.example: I'm sure Riana didn't **mean to upset** you.

rows.use: mean + -ing · involve
rows.example: Being in love **means never having** to say you're sorry.

rows.use: regret + infinitive · be sorry about giving someone bad news (used with verbs such as say, tell, inform, etc.)
rows.example: We **regret to inform** you that the hotel is full.

rows.use: regret + -ing · be sorry about what (has) happened
rows.example: Do you **regret splitting up** with Alec?

rows.use: remember + infinitive · do something you are/were planning to do
rows.example: Did you **remember to order** the flowers?

rows.use: remember + -ing · think of a past event
rows.example: I **don't remember asking** for your opinion.

rows.use: stop + infinitive · interrupt an action to do something else
rows.example: Why didn't you **stop to think** before you acted?

rows.use: stop + -ing · stop an action
rows.example: Will you please just **stop telling** me what to do?

rows.use: try + infinitive · make an effort to achieve something
rows.example: **Try not to forget** her birthday.

rows.use: try + -ing · do something as an experiment to solve a problem
rows.example: You could **try buying** her some flowers.

blocks.text: With some verbs, such as **find, think** or **consider**, it is often possible to use **it** as a preparatory object.

items: **I consider it incredible** that James and Alice are still together.

blocks.text: The subjunctive is a verb form which does not take **-s** in the third person singular. It is possible to use the subjunctive in **that** clauses after words suggesting that something is necessary or preferable.

rows.use: subjunctive
rows.example: The doctor suggested that Sam **take** some time off work. · It is very important that Greg **know** about this.

rows.use: subjunctive of be
rows.example: The subjunctive forms for **be** are **I be, you be**, etc. **It's absolutely essential that I be informed** as soon as the President arrives.

rows.use: should as an alternative
rows.example: The doctor suggested that Sam **(should) take** some time off work.

exercises.title: F · Divorce
exercises.instruction: Tap twelve verbs in the wrong form, then write each one correctly.
exercises.paragraph: Legal and social changes in Britain have led to many more people {click:choosing getting} divorced over the last three decades. The Divorce Reform Act (1969) {click:let people to get} divorced far more easily and, despite {click:promising staying} together for life, over 160,000 couples {click:ended up to get} divorced each year during the late 80s and early 90s, compared to just over 27,000 in 1961. Towards the end of the twentieth century, divorce rates {click:tended falling}, then started to rise again over the first years of the twenty-first century. When asked what {click:motivated them getting} divorced, people usually mention things like {click:not to feel} that the relationship was developing, or their partner {click:making them to feel} inadequate. Whatever {click:causes people separating}, it is often the children who have to {click:learn living} in a different family setting. They often {click:resent to have} to change their lives because the adults involved can't {click:manage resolving} their difficulties. Divorce has got easier legally, but it hasn't got any easier emotionally.
